requirements.heading: Introduction
requirements.text: DNS resolvers and recursive servers MUST support UDP, and SHOULD support TCP, for sending (non-zone-transfer) queries.

requirements.heading: Introduction
requirements.text: This document therefore updates the core DNS protocol specifications such that support for TCP is henceforth a REQUIRED part of a full DNS protocol implementation.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: Section 6.1.3.2 of [RFC1123] is updated: All general-purpose DNS implementations MUST support both UDP and TCP transport.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: o Authoritative server implementations MUST support TCP so that they do not limit the size of responses to what fits in a single UDP packet.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: o Recursive server (or forwarder) implementations MUST support TCP so that they do not prevent large responses from a TCP-capable server from reaching its TCP-capable clients.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: o Stub resolver implementations (e.g., an operating system's DNS resolution library) MUST support TCP since to do otherwise would limit the interoperability between their own clients and upstream servers.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: a DNS resolver or server that is sending a non-zone-transfer query MUST send a UDP query first.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: Stub resolvers and recursive resolvers MAY elect to send either TCP or UDP queries depending on local operational reasons.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: TCP MAY be used before sending any UDP queries.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: If the resolver already has an open TCP connection to the server, it SHOULD reuse this connection.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: In addition, it is noted that all recursive and authoritative servers MUST send responses using the same transport as the query arrived on.

requirements.heading: Transport Protocol Selection
requirements.text: In the case of TCP, this MUST also be the same connection.

requirements.heading: Connection Reuse
requirements.text: To amortise connection setup costs, both clients and servers SHOULD support connection reuse by sending multiple queries and responses over a single persistent TCP connection.

requirements.heading: Connection Reuse
requirements.text: When sending multiple queries over a TCP connection, clients MUST NOT reuse the DNS Message ID of an in-flight query on that connection in order to avoid Message ID collisions.

requirements.heading: Query Pipelining
requirements.text: In order to achieve performance on par with UDP, DNS clients SHOULD pipeline their queries.

requirements.heading: Query Pipelining
requirements.text: When a DNS client sends multiple queries to a server, it SHOULD NOT wait for an outstanding reply before sending the next query.

requirements.heading: Query Pipelining
requirements.text: Clients SHOULD treat TCP and UDP equivalently when considering the time at which to send a particular query.

requirements.heading: Query Pipelining
requirements.text: DNS servers (especially recursive) MUST expect to receive pipelined queries.

requirements.heading: Query Pipelining
requirements.text: The server SHOULD process TCP queries concurrently, just as it would for UDP.

requirements.heading: Query Pipelining
requirements.text: The server SHOULD answer all pipelined queries, even if they are received in quick succession.

requirements.heading: Concurrent Connections
requirements.text: To mitigate the risk of unintentional server overload, DNS clients MUST take care to minimize the number of concurrent TCP connections made to any individual server.

requirements.heading: Concurrent Connections
requirements.text: It is RECOMMENDED that for any given client/server interaction there SHOULD be no more than one connection for regular queries, one for zone transfers, and one for each protocol that is being used on top of TCP (for example, if the resolver was using TLS).

requirements.heading: Concurrent Connections
requirements.text: Similarly, servers MAY impose limits on the number of concurrent TCP connections being handled for any particular client IP address or subnet.

requirements.heading: Concurrent Connections
requirements.text: These limits SHOULD be much looser than the client guidelines above, because the server does not know, for example, if a client IP address belongs to a single client, is multiple resolvers on a single machine, or is multiple clients behind a device performing Network Address Translation (NAT).

requirements.heading: Idle Timeouts
requirements.text: To mitigate the risk of unintentional server overload, DNS clients MUST take care to minimise the idle time of established DNS-over-TCP sessions made to any individual server.

requirements.heading: Idle Timeouts
requirements.text: DNS clients SHOULD close the TCP connection of an idle session, unless an idle timeout has been established using some other signalling mechanism, for example, [edns-tcp-keepalive].

requirements.heading: Idle Timeouts
requirements.text: To mitigate the risk of unintentional server overload, it is RECOMMENDED that the default server application-level idle period be on the order of seconds, but no particular value is specified.

requirements.heading: Idle Timeouts
requirements.text: In practice, the idle period can vary dynamically, and servers MAY allow idle connections to remain open for longer periods as resources permit.

requirements.heading: Idle Timeouts
requirements.text: Servers MAY use zero timeouts when they are experiencing heavy load or are under attack.

requirements.heading: Idle Timeouts
requirements.text: For this reason, servers SHOULD reset the idle timeout on the receipt of a full DNS message, rather than on receipt of any part of a DNS message.

requirements.heading: Teardown
requirements.text: DNS clients SHOULD retry unanswered queries if the connection closes before receiving all outstanding responses.

requirements.heading: Teardown
requirements.text: If a DNS server finds that a DNS client has closed a TCP session (or if the session has been otherwise interrupted) before all pending responses have been sent, then the server MUST NOT attempt to send those responses.

requirements.heading: Teardown
requirements.text: Of course, the DNS server MAY cache those responses.

requirements.heading: Response Reordering
requirements.text: Authoritative servers and recursive resolvers are RECOMMENDED to support the preparing of responses in parallel and sending them out of order, regardless of the transport protocol in use.

requirements.heading: Response Reordering
requirements.text: Stub and recursive resolvers MUST be able to process responses that arrive in a different order than that in which the requests were sent, regardless of the transport protocol in use.

requirements.heading: Response Reordering
requirements.text: In order to achieve performance on par with UDP, recursive resolvers SHOULD process TCP queries in parallel and return individual responses as soon as they are available, possibly out of order.

requirements.heading: Response Reordering
requirements.text: Since pipelined responses can arrive out of order, clients MUST match responses to outstanding queries on the same TCP connection using the Message ID.

requirements.heading: Response Reordering
requirements.text: If the response contains a question section, the client MUST match the QNAME, QCLASS, and QTYPE fields.

requirements.heading: TCP Message Length Field
requirements.text: DNS clients and servers SHOULD pass the two-octet length field, and the message described by that length field, to the TCP layer at the same time (e.g., in a single "write" system call) to make it more likely that all the data will be transmitted in a single TCP segment.

requirements.heading: TCP Message Length Field
requirements.text: To clarify, DNS servers MUST NOT close a connection simply because the first "read" from the TCP layer does not contain the entire DNS message, and servers SHOULD apply the connection timeouts as specified in Section 6.2.3.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Section 6.2.1 adds a new recommendation that TCP connection reuse SHOULD be supported.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Section 6.2.1.1 adds a new recommendation that DNS clients SHOULD pipeline their queries and DNS servers SHOULD process pipelined queries concurrently.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Section 6.2.3 adds a new recommendation that DNS clients SHOULD close idle sessions unless using a signalling mechanism.

requirements.heading: Informative References
requirements.text: Section 7 clarifies that servers are RECOMMENDED to prepare TCP responses in parallel and send answers out of order.
